text: The last two lessons gave you the two numbers that matter most for serving: KV cache memory and how much quantization can shrink the weights. This lesson puts them to work on a question training teams get asked constantly and often can't answer: roughly what will it cost to serve this? You don't need a serving team's precision — you need the order of magnitude and the assumptions behind it.

A serving estimate needs four inputs. Model size and precision set weight memory. Target context length and concurrency set total KV cache memory. GPU memory and its dollar-per-hour cost set what hardware fits and what it costs. And expected throughput — benchmarked on the real stack, not guessed from hardware specs — converts all of that into a cost per token.

Put together: weight memory plus concurrency times per-sequence KV cache memory tells you what hardware you need. Tokens per hour, from measured throughput, divided into the GPU's hourly cost, gives you a cost per million tokens. The exact numbers are illustrative — the shape of the calculation is what transfers to a real model.

Two assumptions dominate and are easiest to get wrong. Throughput, because a naive FLOPs-based calculation routinely overestimates what a real serving stack achieves with real request-length distributions. And concurrency, because planning for average load instead of peak load produces an estimate that looks fine until a real traffic spike blows through the KV cache budget.

This is a planning tool for deciding whether a model is in a reasonable cost range before committing engineering time, and for setting expectations with the team that will serve it — not a substitute for benchmarking the real stack on real hardware. Next up: what a training team actually owes the serving team when handing a model off.
